**3.40**
\textbf{global variable\vRule}
variable whose scope is global

\textbf{3.41}
\textbf{hierarchical addressing}
direct representation of a data element as a member of a physical or logical hierarchy

\textbf{3.42}
\textbf{identifier}
combination of letters, numbers, and underscore characters which begins with a letter or underscore and which names a language element

\textbf{3.43}
\textbf{implementation}
product version of a PLC or the programming and debugging tool provided by the implementer

\textbf{3.44}
\textbf{implementer}
manufacturer of the PLC or the programming and debugging tool provided to the user to program a PLC application

\textbf{3.45}
\textbf{inheritance}
creation of a new class, function block type or interface based on an existing class, function block type or interface, respectively

\textbf{3.46}
\textbf{initial value}
value assigned to a variable at the beginning of its lifetime

\textbf{3.47}
\textbf{in-out variable}
variable which is used to supply a value to a program organization unit and which is additionally used to return a value from the program organization unit

\textbf{3.48}
\textbf{input variable}
variable which is used to supply a value to a program organization unit or method

\textbf{3.49}
\textbf{instance}
individual, named copy of the data structure associated with a function block type, class, or program type

\textbf{3.50}
\textbf{instance name}
identifier associated with a specific instance

\textbf{3.51}
\textbf{instantiation}
creation of an instance

\textbf{3.52}
\textbf{integer literal}
literal which directly represents an integer value

3.78 **resource** + language element corresponding to a signal processing function and its human-machine interface as well as its sensor and actuator interface functions
 
 3.79 **result** + value which is returned as an outcome of a function or method

 3.80 **return** + language construct within a program organization unit designating an end to the execution sequences in the unit

 3.81 **rising** **edge** + change from FALSE(0) to TRUE(1) of a Boolean variable

 3.82 **scope** + set of program organization units within which a declaration or label applies

 3.83 **semantics** + relationships between the symbolic elements of a programming language and their meanings, interpretation and use

 3.84 **semigraphic** representation + representation of graphical information by the use of a limited set of characters

 3.85 **signature** + set of information defining a FUNCTION, FUNCTION BLOCK, or METHODinterface, consisting of an ordered list of parameters and the return type (if any), where each parameter is defined by its name, its type, and its variable-kind (input, output or in-out)

 3.86 **single-element** **variable** + variable which represents a single data element

 3.87 **static** **variable** + variable whose value is stored from one call to the next one

 3.88 **step** + situation in which the behaviour of a program organization unit with respect to its inputs and outputs follows a set of rules defined by the associated actions of the step

 3.89 **structured** **data** **type** + aggregate data type which has been declared using a STRUCTDeclaration

 3.90 **subscripting** + mechanism for referencing an array element by means of an array reference and one or more expressions that, when evaluated, denote the position of the element

## 6 Common elements

### 6.1 Use of printed characters

#### 6.1.1 Character set

Table 1 shows the character set of the textual languages and textual elements of graphical languages. The characters are represented in terms of the ISO/IEC 10646 character set.

#### Table 1 – Character set

| No. |                                | Description                        | 
|-----|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------| 
| 1   | ISO/IEC 10646                     |                                   | 
| 2a  | Lower case characters<sup>a</sup>:    | a, b, c                             | 
| 2b  | Number sign: #                     | See Table 5                          |  
| 2c  | Dollar sign: $                   | See Table 6                          |  
| <sup>a</sup> | When lower-case letters are supported, the case of letters shall not be significant in language elements except within comments as defined in 6.1.5, string literals as defined in 6.3.3, and variables of type STRING, WSTRING and USTRINGS as defined in 6.3.3. |

#### 6.1.2 Identifiers

An identifier is a string of letters, digits, and underscores which shall begin with a letter or underscore character.

The case of letters shall not be significant in identifiers, for example, the identifiers abcd, ABCD, and aBcDshall be interpreted identically.

The underscore character shall be significant in identifiers, for example, A_BcDand AB_Cdshall be interpreted as different identifiers. Multiple leading or multiple embedded underlines are not allowed; for example, the character sequences __L_I_M_S_W_5 and_L_I_M_S_W_5 are not valid identifiers. Trailing underscores are not allowed; for example, the character sequence L_I_M_S_W_5 is not a valid identifier.

At least six characters of uniqueness shall be supported in all systems which support the use of identifiers, for example, ABCDE1shall be interpreted as different from ABCDE2in all such systems. The maximum number of characters allowed in an identifier is an implementer specific dependency.

Identifier features and examples are shown in Table 2.

#### Table 2 – Identifiers

| No. |                          Description | Examples                                        | 
|-----|--------------------------------|----------------------------------------------| 
| 1   | Upper case letters and numbers:| IW215                                        | 
|     |                                | IW215 IW215Z QX75 IIDENT| 
| 2   | Upper and lower case letters, numbers, embedded underscore | ALL THE ABOVE PLUS: LIIM_SW_5 LIM_SW5 abcD ab_Cd | 
| 3   | Upper and lower case, numbers, leading or embedded underscore | ALL THE ABOVE PLUS: MAIN _12V7 |

- A double-byte character string literal is a sequence of zero or more characters from the Basic Multilingual Plane (code point 0 to 65535) of the ISO/IEC 10646 character set. It is prefixed and terminated by the double quote character ("). In double-byte character strings, the five-character combination of the dollar sign \" followed by four hexadecimal digits shall be interpreted as the hexadecimal representation of the sixteen-bit character code, as shown in feature 2h of Table 6.
- A Unicode character string literal is a sequence of zero or more characters from the entire ISO/IEC 10646 character set. It is prefixed by the characters U# and the single quote character (') and terminated by the single quote character ('). Additionally, the prefix characters\string# can be used in place of U# by the implementer. In these literals, the seven-character combination of the dollar sign \" followed by six hexadecimal digits shall be interpreted as the hexadecimal representation of the 24-bit character code, as shown in feature 5e of Table 6.

NOTE 1 Relation of ISO/IEC 10646 and Unicode:

Although the character codes and encoding forms are synchronized between Unicode and ISO/IEC 10646, the Unicode Standard imposes additional constraints on implementations to ensure that they treat characters uniformly across platforms and applications. To this end, it supplies an extensive set of functional character specifications, character data, algorithms and substantial background material that is not in ISO/IEC 10646.

In any string literal the character combinations starting with 'S {' followed by hexadecimal digits and '} shall be interpreted as the hexadecimal representation of the character code as shown in feature 6 of Table 6. It is an error if the escaped character is not representable by the string literal’s type.

### 6.4 Data types

#### 6.4.1 General

A data type is a classification which defines for literals and variables the possible values, the operations that can be done, and the way the values are stored.

#### 6.4.2 Elementary data types (BOOL, INT, REAL, STRING, etc.)

#### 6.4.2.1 Specification of elementary data types

A set of (pre-defined) elementary data types is specified by this document.

Figure 5 – Hierarchy of the generic data types

6.4.4 User-defined data types

6.4.4.1 Declaration (TYPE)

6.4.4.1.1 General

The purpose of the user-defined data types is to be used in the declaration of other data types and in the variable declarations.

A user-defined type can be used anywhere, where a base type can be used.

User-defined data types are declared using the TYPE...END_TYPETextual construct.

A user-defined type declaration consists of

• the name of the type,
• the character “:” (colon), and
• the declaration of the type itself as defined in the following clauses.

EXAMPLE Type declaration

TYPE
  myDatatype1: <data type declaration with optional initialization>;
END_TYPE

6.4.4.1.2 Initialization

The initial value is given by the default initial value, unless a user-defined value is specified.

The user-defined initialization follows the type declaration and starts with the assignment operator “:=” followed by the initial value(s).

Item 1: Introduction

The maximum number of array subscripts, maximum array size and maximum range of subscript values are implementer specific.

The limits of the index subrange(s) shall be literals or constant expressions. Arrays with variable length are defined in 6.5.3.

In the ST language a subscript shall be an expression yielding a value of generic type ANY_INT.

In graphical languages the nominal form of subscripts defined in 8.1.2 is integer literals or single-element variables of generic type ANY_INT.

**EXAMPLE**

a) Declaration of an array

VAR myANALOG 16: ARRAY [1..16] OF ANALOG_DATA
    := [$ (4095), $ (4095)];    // user-defined initial values
END_VAR

b) Usage of array variables in the ST language can be:

OUTARY[$6, SYM]:= INARY[$O] + INARY[$7] - INARY[$l];

**6.4.4.5.2 Initialization**

The default initial value of each array element is the initial value defined for the data type of the array elements.

The user can initialize an array type with a user-defined value. This initialization has priority.

The user-defined initial value of an array is assigned in form of a list which can use parentheses to express repetitions.

During initialization of the array data types, the rightmost subscript of an array shall vary most rapidly with respect to filling the array from the list of initialization values.

**EXAMPLE** Initialization of an array

A: ARRAY [0..5] OF INT:= [2(1, 2, 3)]
   is equivalent to the initialization sequence 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3.

If the number of initial values given in the initialization list exceeds the number of array entries, the excess (rightmost) initial values shall be ignored. If the number of initial values is less than the number of array entries, the remaining array entries shall be filled with the default initial values for the corresponding data type. In either case, the user shall be warned of this condition during preparation of the program for execution.

The user-defined assignment of the initial value of the data type is a feature in Table 11.

**6.4.4.6 Structured data type**

**6.4.4.6.1 General**

The declaration of a structured data type (STRUCT) specifies that this data type shall contain a collection of sub-elements of the specified types which can be accessed by the specified names, as illustrated in Table 11.

◇ More de each image

These rules apply recursively if the type of an element of a structured data type is itself a structured data type.

Formally, let IVDbe the default initial value of a structured data type Sand IVUthe user-defined initial value of S. If Cis a component of Sthat is included in the definition of IVU, the initial value of Cis defined to be the value of Cin IVU. Otherwise, the initial value of Cdefined by IVD.

NOTE Informally, the initial value for a structured data type is the default initial value of the data type, unless specifically overridden for some or all of its elements.

If no user-defined initial value IVU is defined for a structured data type S, the default initial value IVD is used for initialization. If a user-defined initial value IVU is defined that covers all components of S, that value is used for initialization. If a user-defined initial value IVU defined that covers only a part of the components of S, it is used to initialize these components. The default initial value IVV is used to initialize the remaining components. This means that the user-defined initial value IVUoverrides only a part of the default initial value IVV in this case.

EXAMPLE Definition of a structure and initial values

\[\begin{array}{ll}
\text{TYPE} & \\
\text{T : INT := 1; S : STRUCT} & \\
\text{I : T; / / initial value is 1} & \\
\text{J : T := 20; / / initial value is 20} & \\
\text{K : T := 30; / / initial value is 30} & \\
\text{L : T := 40; / / initial value is 40} & \\
\text{END\_STRUCT;} & \\
\text{U : S := (K := 300); / / initial values are (I = 1, J = 20, K = 300, L = 40)} & \\
\text{V : U := (L := 4000); / / initial values are (I = 1, J = 20, K = 300, L = 4000)} & \\
\text{END\_TYPE}
\end{array}\]

The initial value 1 of the element I is its default initial value, which is the initial value of T.

The initial value 2 of the element J is its user-defined initial value.

The initial value (I := 1, J := 20, K := 30, L := 40) of the structural type S is its default initial value, which is constituted by the initial values of its elements.

The initial value (I := 1, J := 20, K := 300, L := 40) of U is composed of its default initial value, which is the initial value of S and of U’s user-defined initial value, which is (K := 300). The latter takes precedence.

The initial value (I := 1, J := 20, K := 300, L := 4000) of V is composed of its default initial value, which is the initial value of V and of V’s user-defined initial value, which is (L := 4000). The latter takes precedence.

6.4.4.7 Relative location for elements of structured data types (AT)

6.4.4.7.1 General

The locations (addresses) of the elements of a structured type can be defined relative to the beginning of the structure.

In this case the name of each component of this structure shall be followed by the keyword AT and a relative location. The declaration can contain gaps in the memory layout.

The relative location consists of a ‘%’ (percent), the location qualifier and a bit or byte location. A byte location is an unsigned integer literal denoting the byte offset. A bit location consists of a byte offset, followed by a ‘:’ (point), and the bit offset as unsigned integer literal out of the range of 0 to 7. White spaces are not allowed within the relative location.

6.4.4.7.2 Initialization

Overlapped structures cannot be initialized explicitly.

6.4.4.8 Directly represented components of a structure – partly specified using “*”

The asterisk notation “*” in Table 11 can be used to denote not yet fully specified locations for directly represented components of a structure.

: Assigning of the components of a structure to not yet located inputs and outputs.

TYPE
**HW_Comp: STRUCT**
IN : *1: BOOL;
VAL : *1: WORD;
OUT : *0: C0;
OUT : *0: C0;
**AND_STR**: REAL;
END STR;**E_

In the case that a directly represented component of a structure is used in a location assignment in the declaration part of a program, a function block type, or a class, an asterisk “*” shall be used in place of the size prefix and the unsigned integer(s) in the concatanation to indicate that the direct representation is not yet fully specified.

The use of this feature requires that the location of the structured variable so declared shall be fully specified inside the VAR_CONFIG...END_VARconstrUON of the configuration for every instance of the containing type.

Variables of this type shall not be used in a VAR_INPUT, VAR_IN_OUT, or VAR_TEMPersecting.

### 6.5.3 Variable length ARRAYvariables

**Variable-length arrays can only be used**

* as input or in-out variables of functions and methods,
* as in-out variables of programs and function blocks.

**NOTE The restriction enables an implementer to use call-by-reference semantics and reflects the call-site-specific size of the array.**

The count of array dimensions of actual and formal parameter shall be the same. They are specified using an asterisk as an undefined subrange specification for the index ranges.

**Variable-length arrays provide the means for programs, functions, function blocks, and methods to use arrays of different index ranges.**

The counting of array dimensions starts with index 1. It is an error if a non-existing dimension is supplied as input parameter DIMfor the functions LOWER_BOUND and UPPER_BOUND.

To handle variable-length arrays, the following functions shall be provided, see Table 15.

**Table 15 – Variable-length ARRAYvariables**

| No. | Description | Examples |
|----|-------------|---------|
| 1   | Declaration using *<br>    **ARRAY \[*,*,...,\]* OF data type | VAR_IN_OUT <br>  A: ARRAY \[*,*,*\]* OF INT; <br> END VAR |
| 2a  | Functions LOWER_BOUND / UPPER_BOUND |         |
|    | Graphical representation | Get lower bound of an array: <br>    +-------------------------! <br>    LOWER_BOUND ! <br>  ARRAY ---------! ARR <br>    | ANY_INT! --> DIM <br>  +-------------------------! <br> Get upper bound of an array: <br>    +-------------------------! <br>  UPPER_BOUND ! <br>  ARRAY -----! ARR <br>    | ANY_INT! --> DIM <br>  +-------------------------! |
| 2b  | Textual representation | Get lower bound of the second dimension of the array A: <br>  low2 := LOWER_BOUND (A, 2) ; <br> Get upper bound of the second dimension of the array A: <br>  up2 := UPPER_BOUND (A, 2) ; |

```
      FUNCTION SUM: INT;
       VAR_IN_OUT A: ARRAY \[*\] OF INT; END_VAR
       i, sum2: INT; END_VAR
       sum2:= 0;
       FOR i:= LOWER_BOUND(A,1) TO UPPER_BOUND(A,1)
        sum2:= sum2 + A[i];
       END_FOR;
       SUM:= sum2;
       END_FUNCTION

**6.5.5.3** **Declaration of variables as aliases to directly represented variables (AT)**

A variable can be declared to be an alias to a directly represented variable, as defined in Table 16, using the ATkeyword.

Variables with user-defined data types e.g. an array can be assigned an absolute memory by using AT. Implicit and explicit data type conversion may be applied to adapt the data type of the source to the data type of the target:

a) In textual form (also partially applicable to graphical languages) the assignment operator may be

“:=” which means the value of the expression on the right side of the operator is written to the variable on the left side of the operator or

“=>” which means the value on the left side of the operator is written to the variable on the right side of the operator.

The “=>” operator is only used in the parameter list of calls of functions, methods, function blocks, etc. and only to pass \textit{VAR_OUTPUT} parameter back to the caller.

\textbf{EXAMPLE}

A :=  B  +  C / 2;
func (in1 := A, out2 => x);
	A_struct1 := B_struct1;

\textbf{NOTE} For assignment of user-defined data types (struct, Array) see Table 71.

b) In graphical form the assignment is visualized as a graphical connection line from a source to a target, in principle from left to right; e.g. from a function block output to a function block input or from the graphical location of a variable or constant to a function input or from an function output to the graphical location of a variable.

The standard function \textbf{MOVE} is one of the graphical representations of an assignment.

\textbf{6.6.1.2.3 Expression}

An expression is a language construct that consists of a defined combination of operands, like literals, function calls, and operators like ( +, -, *, /) and yields one value.

Implicit and explicit data type conversion may be applied to adapt the data types of an operand of the expression.

a) In textual form (also partially applicable in graphical languages), the expression is executed in a defined order depending on the precedence as specified in the language.

\textbf{EXAMPLE} . . . A  +  B  +  C / 2 * \textbf{SIN}(x) . . .

b) In graphical form, the expression is visualized as a network of graphical blocks (function blocks, functions, etc.) connected with lines.

\textbf{6.6.1.2.4 Constant expression}

A constant expression is a language construct that consists of a defined combination of operands like literals, constant variables, enumerated or named values and operators like ( +, -, *, AND, OR, etc.) and yields one value.

### 6.6.1.4.3 Graphical languages  
In the graphical languages the call of functions shall be represented as graphical blocks according to the following rules:

1. The form of the block shall be rectangular.  
2. The size and proportions of the block may vary depending on the number of inputs and other information to be displayed.  
3. The direction of processing through the block shall be from left to right (input parameters on the left and output parameters on the right).  
4. The name or symbol of the called entity, as specified below, shall be located inside the block.  
5. Provision shall be made for input and output variable names appearing at the inside left and right sides of the block respectively.  
6. An additional input `ENOR` output `ENOOR` both may be used. If present, they shall be shown at the uppermost positions at the left and right side of the block, respectively.  
7. The function result shall be shown at the uppermost position at the right side of the block, except if there is an `ENOU` output, in which case the function result shall be shown at the next position below the `ENO` output. Since the name of the called entity itself is used for the assignment of its output value, no output variable name shall be shown at the right side of the block, i.e., for the function result.  
8. Parameter connections (including function result) shall be shown by signal flow lines.  
9. Negation of Boolean signals shall be shown by placing an open circle just outside of the input or output line intersection with the block. In the character set this may be represented by the upper case alphabetic “○”, as shown in Table 20. The negation is performed outside the POU.  
10. All inputs and outputs (including function result) of a graphically represented function shall be represented by a single line outside the corresponding side of the block, even though the data element may be a multi-element variable.  
11. Results and outputs (`VAR_OUTPUT`) can be connected to a variable, used as input to other calls, or can be left unconnected.

As shown in Table 18, an additional Boolean EN(Enable) input or ENO(Enable Out) output, or both, can
be provided by the implementer or the user according to the declarations.
```
VAR_INPUT EN: BOOL:= 1; END_VAR
VAR_OUTPUT ENO: BOOL; END_VAR

```
When these variables are used, the execution of the operations defined by the POU shall be controlled
according to the following rules:
```
1) If the value of ENIS FALSE (0) then the POU shall not be executed. In addition, ENOshall be reset to
  FALSE. The implementer shall specify the behaviour in this case in detail, see the examples below.
2) Otherwise, if the value of ENIS TRUE, the value TRUEIS assigned to ENO, followed by an execution
  of the POU implementation. During this execution, a different value may be assigned to ENO.
3) If any error occurs during the execution of a POU, the ENOutput of that POU shall be reset to
  FALSE(0) by the programmable controller system, or the implementer shall specify other
  disposition of such an error.
4) If the ENOoutput is evaluated to FALSE(0), the values of all POU outputs (VAR_OUTPUT,
  VAR_IN_OUT and function result) are implementer specific.
5) The input ENshall only be set as an actual value as a part of a call of a POU.

```

Figure 12 shows the data type conversions which are supported by implicit type conversion. The arrows present the possible conversion paths; e.g. BOOL can be converted to BYTE, BYTE can be converted to WORD, etc.

Figure 12 - Implicit type conversions overview

The following example shows examples of the data type conversion.

**EXAMPLE 6** Explicit vs. implicit type conversion

1. Type declaration

```
VAR
  PartsRatePerHr: REAL;
  PartsDone: INT;
  HoursElapsed: REAL;
  PartsPerShift: INT;
  ShiftLength: SIN;
END_VAR
```

2. Usage in ST language

a) Explicit type conversion

```
PartsRatePerHr:= INT_TO_REAL(PartsDone) / HoursElapsed; PartsPerShift:= REAL_TO_INT(SINTO_REAL(ShiftLength)*PartsRatePerHr);
```

b) Explicit overloaded type conversion

```
PartsRatePerHr:= TO_REAL(PartsDone) / HoursElapsed; PartsPerShift:= TO_INT(TO_REAL(ShiftLength)*PartsRatePerHr);
```

c) Implicit type conversion

```
PartsRatePerHr:= PartsDone / HoursElapsed; PartsPerShift:= TO_INT(ShiftLength * PartsRatePerHr);
// the * operation is done in REAL, the operand ShiftLength is //
implicitly converted to REAL beforehand
```

### EXAMPLE 2

This document defines for the bit-shift function SHL.the generic data type ANY_BITfor one input and the result output and the generic data type ANY_INT for another input.
The implementer specifies for these two generic data types of the PLC system:
ANY_BITrepresents e.g. the elementary data types BYTEand WORD;
ANY_INTrepresents e.g. the elementary data types INT and LINT.

An overloaded language element shall operate on the defined elementary data types according to the following rules:

- The data types of inputs, outputs and result shall be of the same type; this is applicable for the inputs, outputs and result of the same kind.
- The same kind means parameters, operands and the result equally used like the inputs of an addition or multiplication.
- More complex combinations shall be implementer specific.
- If the data types of the inputs and outputs of the same kind have not the same type, then the conversion in the language element is implementer specific.
- The implicit type conversion of an expression and of the assignment follows the sequence of evaluation of the expression. See example below.
- The data type of the variable to store the result of the overloaded function does not influence the data type of the result of the function or operation.

**NOTE** The user can explicitly specify the result type of the operation by using typed functions.

#### EXAMPLE 3

```
int3::=int1  +int2; (* Addition is performed as an integer operation *)
dint1:=int1  +int2; (* Addition is performed as an integer operation, then the result is converted to a DINT and assigned to dint1 *)
dint1:=dint2  +int3; (* int3 is converted to a DINT, the addition is performed as a DINT addition *)
```
If an overloaded function is called, its signature is chosen such that the call is valid according to the rules for non-overloaded functions. It is an error if there is no such signature. If the call includes untyped literals as actual parameters, the typing is implementer specific.

If there are multiple signatures that satisfy this condition, the smallest is used. A signature `xixis` smaller than a signature `Yif for each parameter` `Pxof` `X` there is an equally named parameter `PY`in and `PX's` type is implicitly convertible into that of `PY`. It is an error if there is no smallest signature.

#### EXAMPLE 4

The `SUBfunction` has signatures `TXTT->T`, where `Tis` one of the `ANY_NUMBERtypes`. For the call
```
  `SUB(INT#1, DINT#1)`

the following signatures can be applied:

`SUB: DINT x DINT -> DINT SUB:
LINT x LINT -> LINT SUB:
LREAL x LREAL -> LREAL`

The first signature is the smallest, since `DINTis` implicitly convertible into `LINTand` `LREAL`.

- Do not remove reports, simulation results, source codes from the in-use environment.

6.6.2.5 Standard functions

6.6.2.5.1 General

A standard function specified in 6.6.2.5 to be extensible is allowed to have two or more inputs to which the indicated operation is to be applied, for example, extensible addition shall give at its output the sum of all its inputs. The actual number of inputs effective in a formal call of an extensible function is determined by the formal input name with the highest position in the sequence of variable names.

How can I extract a value from the text using the BOoLused software?To extract a value from the text using BOoLused, follow these steps: 1) Find the range of the specific value you want to extract in all rows. 2) Identify the needed fields and convert them into decimal numbers. 3) Find the appropriate decimal number that corresponds to the specific required value. 4) Enter this decimal number as a decimal number in the first cell of the new row and copy it to populate it with an accurate decimal number. 5) Repeat the whole process for all the relevant decimal numbers.

6.6.2.5.5 Data type conversion between bit types and numeric types

These data type conversions use the following rules:

1) Data type conversion is done as binary copy.

2) If the source data type is smaller than the target data type the source value is stored into the least

significant bytes of the target variable and the most significant bytes are set to zero.

EXAMPLE l

X: SINT:= 18; W: WORD; W:= SINT_TO_WORD(X); // W contains 18 (16#0012)

3) If the source data type is bigger than the target data type only the least significant bytes of the

source variable are stored into the target data type.

EXAMPLE 2

W:WORD:= 16#1234; X: SINT; X:=WORDTO_SINT(W);//X contains 52 (16#34) .

## II. NEC Performance: Warranty of Continuity of Title

Customer warranty is intended to expressly extend to a right to consideration, reimbursement, or performance of the selling transaction. Customer warranty includes the following explicit obligations:

- Warranty period: One year (the original term stated in the customer sales contract).
- Scope of coverage: The sale just includes (electrical) wiring.
- Accuracy: If there is a particular software in the transaction, the software defined products required by party A.

### TYPES OF WARRANTIES

- **Build and wiring warranty: See clause 7.3**
  - This warranty covers copper wiring, so that the seller will carry the risk for faults in copper wiring. (But missing copper wiring might not automatically lead to the buyer holding a claim under Clause 11.2)
- **Hardware listing warranty: Manufacturer warranty**
  - This warranty concerns the hardware supplied with the computer. When claimed it can extend up to 12 months (if the stated warranty has expired, excludes the clause of other warranties).
- **Charges: Under clause 6.10 and 7.29**

### TERMS & CONDITIONS

- **Validity: Effective as of October 15, 2022**
  - This term ensures that the buyer-LUC refers to all assets before October 15, 2022, any sales tax and municipal taxes, etc.
- **Subject: Includes all goods and services**
  - This clause defines who falls within the product list and their affiliation.
- **Charges: Before October 15, 2022**
  - The seller must cover the cost of goods available in any outlet up to MSRP of your local PT stock.
- **Country of Purchase of Goods: China**
  - The seller should be able to import this product any time after the purchase date.
- **Vehicle: Vehicles**: **hosts the seizure of the vehicle, and the damage caused by storms, floods, public liability, damage to third parties, and damage resulting from vagrancy.**
  - Changes in certain circumstances are not considered to be the fault. The seller must provide proof of depreciation.
- **Delivery: 25 October 2022**
  - This is the deadline at which the way bills will appear. Any payment below this can be removed by the way bills (A and B).

## IV. Purchase Price & Processing Charges

- **Regarding Price: The final acceptable selling price is鲜活 goods at the buyer's expense including VAT, and Direct Tax, including industry characteristics and rational prices: OSDP.**
  - This clause also states that the price includes a 5% VAT. The term of 'virgin' goods in material quality means that the seller is fully responsible for quality, and does not make supplementary quality claims. OSDP is a turnover tax.
- **Partial delivery: Not included**
  - Not included means, e.g., a website is available, reviewer fees and the like.
- **Included after 25/01/2023 at receiver's expense: If the acid neutralizer is removed.**
  - Changes in the setting environment can render the supplier unable to meet the terms, and the goal of minimizing damage during exchange is achieved by purchasing stolen goods and declaring them with low prices as a means of exchange. ## Table 30 – Bit shift functions

Let's consider the following baseline implementation and note its zero-based count.

For Blitz (an automatic code generator for Tiny Tiny Tiny), the specific bit shift function number is 606, as seen in Table 30 (not the full module).

\[\text{Bit Shift Function Number} = 606\]

This function will be used later in a conditional structure:
\[\begin{align*}
\text{Evaluate bool} &= (\text{Expression1} \neq \text{Expression\ 2}) \\
&= (\text{Expression1} \neq \text{Expression\ 2}) &&=\ \text{Bit Shift} &&\left( \frac{\text{Expression1} && \text{Expression\ 2}}{\text{Expression\ 1} - \text{Expression\ 2}} \right) &&\ left \&&&& \& \&&\\
&= &\text{False} &&\ &= \left| \begin{array}{cc}
\text{Expression1} && \text{Statement}
\end{array} \right| &&\ \text{Expression\ 1} && \text{Else} && \left( \frac{\text{Expression1} - \text{Expression\ 2}}{\text{Expression\ 1} - \text{Expression\ 2}} \right) &&&& \text{Else} && \left( \frac{\text{Expression1} - \text{Expression\ 2}}{\text{Expression\ 1} - \text{Expression\ 2}} \right) &&&\left|
\end{align*}\]

For the conditional statement mentioned above, the code snippet would be:

```c
if(Expression1 || Expression2) {
  // Code to be executed
}
```

Similarly, the bit shift function for `4` in the idiom below would be:

```c
  4) << 1) /* calculates the value to shift */
```

while the corresponding bit shift function for `2` would be:

```c
  2) >> 1) /* calculates the value to shift */
```

As for optimize versions, one could consider usingShiftDocumentation to uniformly wrap the various bit shift functions in a module, potentially helped by ending up with a similar structure to Blitz's in C. Alternatively, as suggested by Bill Anzick, it might be possible to recognize that the majority of bit shift functions in ZERO are simply variations of the standard binary shift functions. This approach could lead to a simpler, more generalized solution and more precise type-safety checks.

6.6.2.5.12 Character string functions

The standard graphical representations, function names and descriptions of additional functions of character strings shall be as shown in Table 34. • the arguments of data type STRING/CHAR, WSTRING/WCHAR, or USTRING/UCHAR are mixed at the same function.

The following data types shall be supported as inputs or outputs of the endianness conversion functions:

- ANY_INTWITH size greater than or equal to 16 bits

- ANY_DATE
- arrays of these data types
- structures containing components of these data types as long as these components do not overlap (see 6.4.4.7)
- subranges and named values data types according to their base data type

The application of endianness conversion on a value of type array or structure is defined as the recursive application of the endianness conversion on its elements or members.

在编程语言中，函数被用于进行某些明确操作。在旧技术中，这些操作被保留为一个小型，在很小的范围内使用，并根据需要扩展它们的大小（因为这些操作不必在一个应用程序中重复）。这就是我们得到的小型的函数的情况。

函数被设计为在任务代码中紧密相关的能力是有用的，或者能够在较短的时间内完成（具有相对较小的签名或值类型）。因此，它们在参数中使用逗号拆分参数（如函数 f 中）

虽然函数名称也必须在参数中列出（如在 f 中），但它们并没有像C++或 C# 的命名空间中的那样，是一种特殊的输出变量。

**They indicate that a variable can仅在参数中有值，但这不能用作名称空间中的名称成员。**

Deferred state machines 是一种行为主义。

**对函数标记：--，***

**输入：@ 输出：@ 输入-输出：@

**输出：**`与输入-类型-类型-输出 ……X正式输入`

**And输入-输出：** `@ + 形成输出-类型-输出-输出 ……X正式输入`

图1：可以（但不是必须的）识别函数块的输入-输出由“标识符”表示，由虚线表示。虽然输出随机意味着“名称空间中的名称”。

---

d) 有作用的函数

Deferred state machines 的第二个特征 “状态变化”。通过使一个函数从一个状态移动到另一个状态（无论是否是最终目标），deferred state machines 展示了一些子类型的状态变化，那些持续一段时间（即超依依特化）：

---

增值税和消费税的数值可以发生变化，在数学计算中专业系统会根据需要发生变化（即使它是不可变的）。

```

### 相关应用

**概念分离：是用于避免一个功能不变的子函数或测试自动扩展（可访问该文本的以下关键段落）**

**语言：C#**

```

---

功能分离是标准化的，通过可观察到的属性的组合使管理任务更易于。这使得在设计的第一个表现形式中更容易创建和应用功能。

---

理解了 Deferred state machines，使这些变化成为可能将释放一种或另一种基于兴趣的缩写/大写的无穷资产的可能性，如“逻辑/脚本设备” 。

As shown in Table 42, a function block instance shall be declared in a similar manner as described for structured variables.

The provisions of the initial values of structured data type (see



6.4.4.2) also apply to the initial values of function block instances with the following restriction: user-defined initial values are limited to input, output, or public variables of the function block instance.

# 6 . 6 . 5 Classes

6 . 6 . 5 . 1 General

The language element class supports the object-oriented paradigm, and is characterized by the following concepts :

- classes, consisting of methods (algorithms) and data structures ;
- definitions of data structures partitioned into public and nonpublic variables ; •
methods and properties that operate on instances of the data structure ;
- interfaces with method prototypes and implementation of interfaces ; •
inheritance of interfaces and classes ;
- instantiation of classes .

NOTE The terms class and object used in IT programming languages like C#, C++, Java, UML etc., correspond to the terms type and instance used in PLC programming languages of this document. This is shown below .

### Page 136

value into the security process.

1. IT programming languages: C#, C++, Java, UML   - Class = type of an object  
2. Object = instance of a class   

PLC languages of this document   
- Function block type or class type   
- Instance of a function block or a class   

![Figure 19 illustrates the inheritance of interface (see 6.6.6) and classes using the mechanisms of implementation and extension. ]  

Figure 19 - Interface and Interface Implementation   
    A class is a POU designed for object-oriented programming. A class contains essentially variables and methods. A class shall be instantiated before its methods can be called or its variables can be accessed.   

6.6.5.2 Class declaration   
The features of the class declaration are defined in Table 49.  

The rules listed below shall be followed when declaring a class:  

1. The keyword CLASS, followed by an identifier specifying the name of the class being declared.  
2. The terminating keyword END_CLASS.  
3. The values of the variables that are declared via a VAR_EXTERNAL construct can be read and written from within the class.  
4. The values of the constants that are declared via a VAR_EXTERNAL CONSTANT construct can only be read from within the class.  
5. A VAR...END_VARconstruct is used to specify the names and types of the static variables of the class.  
6. Variables are initialized according to 6.5.1.3.  
7. Variables of the VARSection can be declared PUBLIC. A public variable can be accessed from outside the class.  
8. The RETAINOR NON_RETAINqualifier can be used for variables of a class.  
9. The asterisk '* notation as defined in Table 16 can be used in the declaration of variables of a class.  
10. Variables can be PUBLIC, PRIVATE, INTERNAL, or PROTECTED. The access specifier PROTECTEDis default.  
11. A class can extend another class. The derived class inherits variables and methods from the base class. Furthermore, the derived class can also introduce new functionality in addition to the base class.

**EXAMPLE**  
**Class declaration**

**CLASS**  
**CCounter**  
VAR  
  m_iCurrentValue: INT; (* Default = 0 *)  
  m_bCountUp: BOOL:= TRUE;  
END_VAR  

VAR  
  PUBLIC  
    m_iUpperLimit: INT:= +10000;  
    m_iLowerLimit: INT:= -10000;  
END_VAR  

METHOD Count (* Only body *)  
  IF (m_bCountUp AND m_iCurrentValue < m_iUpperLimit) THEN  
    m_iCurrentValue:= m_iCurrentValue+1;  
  END{_IF;}  
  IF (NOT m_bCountUp AND m_iCurrentValue > m_iLowerLimit) THEN  
    m_iCurrentValue:= m_iCurrentValue-1;  
  END{_IF;}  

END_METHOD  

**METHOD**  
**SetDirection**

    BOOL;  
  END_VAR  
  m_bCountUp:= bcCountUp;  

END_METHOD  

**Method**  
**SetDirection**

bcCountUp:  
  BOOL;  
END_VAR

END_METHOD

**6.6.5.3**  
**Class instance declaration**

The declaration of a class instance is the same as the declaration of a structured variable.

For initialization, the rules defined for structured values (6.4.4.6.2) apply, with the addition that access specifiers shall be followed as shown in Table 50. Outside of a class-declaration, user-defined initial values can only be defined for public variables of that class.

**Table 50 – Class instance declaration**

| No. | Description | Example |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| 1   | Declaration of class instance initialized using the initial value of the class type | VARSYMARY  
  MyCounter1: CCounter;  
END_VAR |
| 2   | Declaration of class instance initialized using used-defined values of public variables | VARSYMARY  
  MYCOUNTER2:-  
  CCounter:= (m_iUpperLimit:= 20000,  
-20000) m_iLowerLimit:= -20000);  
END_VAR |

value of helpful answers.6.6.5.4 Methods of a class

6.6.5.4.1 General

For the purpose of programming PLCs, the concept of methods, as generally known in object-oriented programming, is adopted as a set of optional language elements defined within the class definition.

Methods can be used to define the operations to be performed on the class instance data.

6.6.5.4.2 Signature

In the context of this document the term signature is a set of information defining unambiguously the identity of the parameter interface of a method.

A signature consists of an ordered list of parameters and the return type (if any), where each parameter is defined by its name, its type, and its variable-kind (input, output or in-out).

Temporary variables are not a part of the signature. The same holds for variables defined in a `VAR_EXTERNAL` section and constant variables.

The access specifiers, like `PUBLIC PORIVATE`, are not relevant for the signature.

6.6.5.4.3 Method declaration and execution

A class can have a set of methods.

The declaration of a method shall comply with the following rules:

1) Methods are declared within the scope of a class.
2) A method can be defined in any of the programming languages specified in this document.
3) In the textual declaration the methods are listed after the declaration of the variables of the class.
4) A method can declare its own `VAR_INPUT`, `VAR_TEMP`, `VAR_OUTPUT`, `VAR_IN_OUT`, `VAR_EXTERNALsections` and optionally a method result type.
5) The keywords `VAR_TEMPD` and `VARhave` the same meaning and both are used to declare temporary variables.
6) The method declaration can contain one of the following access specifiers: `PUBLIC`, `PRIVATE`, `INTERNAL`, and `PROTECTED`. If no access specifier is given, the method will be `PROTECTEDby default`.
7) The method declaration can contain the additional keywords `OVERRIDE`, `ABSTRACT` or `FINAL`.

NOTE 1 Overloading of methods is not in the scope of this document.

The execution of a method shall comply with the following rules:

1) The method result is assigned to the method name.
2) All method variables and the result are temporary (like the variables of a function). That is the values are not stored from one method execution to the next.
3) The variable names of each method and of the class shall be unique in the scope of the class.
4) The names of local variables of different methods can be the same.
5) All methods have read and write access to the static and external variables declared in the class.

}^ \) value is defended by default. In the code, it can be seen that a local variable declared in a function is available to the scope of the function where it is declared.

For example, `a` is visible in the `main` function but not in the `sub1` function. On the other hand, `b` is available to the `sub1` function because it is enclosed within the `if` statement in the `sub1` function. Finally, `c` is also visible to the `main` function, but it is not visible to the `sub1` function. This is because `c` is declared in the `if` statement and can only be accessed within the `if` statement.

In summary, local variables are variables that are declared within a specific function and cannot be accessed outside that function. This helps maintain the scope and control of variables within a program.

Local variables in named parameters are also known as hidden parameters. These are parameters that are declared within a function but not visible to the function to which they are passed. The `hidden` modifier is used to identify and manage hidden parameters in C programs.

The following code illustrates the differences between local and global variables:

```cpp
// Example of local and global variables
// hour is a global variable defined outside the scope of the function
int hour;

void my_func() {
    // This is a local variable declared inside the function
    int hour = 4;

    // Accessing the local variable within the function
    printf("The time is %d hours.\n", hour);
}

// The following code is an example of accessing a local variable outside the function
void my_func_without_hidden() {
    int hour;

    // This works because `hour` is not a hidden parameter
    hour = 4;
}

// The following code is an example of accessing a global variable outside the function
int main() {
    printf("The time is %d hours.\n", get_hour());
}

char get_hour() {
    return 'H';
}
```

In this example, the `hours` variable is declared inside the `my_func` function and is a global variable with a value of `4`. In the `main` function, we access the `hours` variable using the `printf` and `get_hour` functions.

The following code is an example of accessing a local variable within a function:

```cpp
// Example of local and global variables
// hours is a local variable defined inside the function
int hours;

void my_func() {
    // This is a local variable declared inside the function
    int hours = 4;

    // Accessing the local variable within the function
    printf("The time is %d hours.\n", hours);
}

// The following code is an example of accessing a local variable outside the function
void my_func_without_hidden() {
    int hours;

    // This works because `hours` is defined in the local scope
    hours = 4;
}

// The following code is an example of accessing a global variable outside the function
int main() {
    printf("The time is %d hours.\n", get_hour());
}

char get_hour() {
    return 'H';
}
```

In this example, the `hours` variable is declared inside the `my_func` function and is a local variable with a value of `4`. In the `main` function, we access the `hours` variable using the `printf` and `get_hour` functions.

**6.6.5.10 Variable Access Specifics (Protected, Public, Private, Internal)**

For the VArsection it shall be defined through the access of the variables of this section as permitted. The accessibility of the variables is defined by using one of the following access specifies following the keyword VAR.

**NOTE**: The access specifics can be combined with qualifiers like return const AnsWaniy any order.

- **PROTECTED**

  If inheritance is supported the access specific PROTECTED is applicable. It indicates for variables that they are only accessible from inside the variable’s class and from inside all derived classes. PROTECTED easily default and may be omitted.

  If inheritance is implemented but not used, PROTECTED has the same effect as PRIVATE.

  **PUBLIC**

  The access specific PUB LI Cindicates for variables that they are accessible at any place where the class can be used.

- **PRIVATE**

  The access specific PRIV AT E indicates for variables that they are only accessible from inside the variable’s class.

- **INTERNAL**

  If namespace is supported the access specific INTERNAL is applicable. It indicates for variables that they are only accessible from within the NAMES PACE, in which the variable’s class is declared.

All improper uses shall be treated as errors.

6.6.5.11.2 Declaration  
A property is declared by a get method and a set method.
The declaration of a get method for an identifier P is equal to the declaration of a method P, with the following differences:
• The keyword PROPERTY_GET is used instead of the keyword METHOD.
• The keyword END_PROPERTY is used instead of the keyword END_METHOD.
• The return-type is the property's type. The type of the property shall be defined.
  • A variable with the property's name and type is implicitly defined in the scope of the property's body. An assignment to this variable specifies the return value of the get method.
• VAR_INPUT, VAR_OUTPUT, and VAR_INOUT sections shall not be defined as part of the property. Thus, only VAR, VAR_TEMPAND VAR_EXTERNAL sections are allowed.
NOTE 1 Usually the get method is programmed such that it does not change the state of its associated object, since the readaccess on a variable also has no side-effect.
The declaration of a set method is equal to the declaration of a get method with the following differences:
• The keyword PROPERTY_SET is used instead of the keyword PROPERTY_GET.
• The implicitly defined variable is constant. Its value is defined by the input parameter when it is called.
The declaration of the get method is optional, and the declaration of the set method is optional for a property P. If both are defined, the property type shall be equal in both declarations.
NOTE 2 The rules for name conflicts, abstract methods, accessspecifications, method prototypes etc. also apply to properties.
6.6.5.11.3 Usage of properties
Let Abe a class, function block, or interface that defines a property P and let X be an expression of type A.
The assignment X.P :=V is semantically equivalent to the call of P's set method with V as input parameter for the call. The same holds for the assignment attempt (X.P :=V) and the assignment from a formal output parameter V to the actual parameter (V=>X.P). The rules for method calls apply.
If a property is used as described, it shall be an error if its set method is not defined.
The use of X.P in a context where an expression is expected is semantically equivalent to the call of P's get method, with the result being used as the call's value. The rules for method calls apply.
If a property is used as described, it shall be an error if its get method is not defined.
It shall be an error if X.P is referenced or is used as actual parameter for a VAR_IN_OUT variable.
NOTE The rules for accessrestrictions etc. also apply to properties.
It is an error if the get or set method of a property is called in any other way, in particular if it is called using the syntax of a method call.

## A. Limitations

### Multiple Copies

One might argue that the predictions for the same patient are **merely** different cases. In actual fact, the data on each patient is quite different. The genotypes and phenotypes may be highly correlated, which consequently make predictions difficult from a PSMD perspective. We do not have the interpretation of the genotype and phenotype, but save it for the future discussion.

### Missed Data

There exists a critical number of missing data for the individual genotypes and phenotypes. Below is the missing data for one of these genotypes:

rm(list = ls());

### 6.6.6.2 Use of interface

An interface type can be used in two ways:
a. **In a class declaration:**
    This specifies which methods the class shall implement; e.g., for reuse of the interface specification as illustrated in Figure 21.
   
b. **As a type of a variable:**
    - A variable whose type is interface contains either the value `NULL` or references an instance of a class that implements the interface.
    - It is an error if a method is called on the interface value `NULL`.

Interfaces shall not be used as in-out variables.

#### Table 52 – Interface

| No. | Description | Explanation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | INTERFACE ... END_INTERFACE | Interface definition |
| Methods |   |   |
| 2 | METHOD... END_METHOD | Method prototype definition |
| Inheritance |   |   |
| 3 | EXTENDS | Interface inherits from interface |
| Usage of interface |   |   |
| 4a | IMPLEMENTS interface | Implements an interface in a class declaration |
| 4b | IMPLEMENTS multiple interfaces | Implements more than one interface in a class declaration |
| 4c | Interface as type of a variable | Referecing an implementation (class or function block instance) of the interface |
| Properties |   |   |
| 5a | PROPERTY_SET...END_PROPERTY | Definition of a property get prototype |
| 5b | PROPERTY_SET...END_PROPERTY | Definition of a property set prototype |

#### 6.6.6.3 Method prototype

A method prototype is a restricted method definition for the use in an interface definition.

It contains the method name, `VAR_INPUT`, `VAR_OUTPUT` and `VAR_IN_OUT` variables and optionally a return type. A method prototype definition does not contain any algorithm (code) or temporary variables, i.e. it does not yet include the implementation.

A function block type can have a function block body and additionally a set of methods. Since the FB body or the methods or both may be omitted, there are three variants of function block types. This is shown in the example in Figure 23.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Function block type with a FB body only.
  \begin{itemize}
    \item This function block type is known from IEC 61131-3:2003.
    In this case the function block type has no methods implemented. The elements of the function block type (inputs, outputs, etc.) and the call of the function block instance are shown in the example in Figure 23 a).
  \end{itemize}
\item Function block type with methods and an empty FB body.
\begin{itemize}
  \item In this case this function block type can also be declared as a class. The elements of the function block type and the call of a method are shown in the example in Figure 23 b)).
\item Function block type with methods and a non-empty FB body.
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item Methods shall support the access to their own locally defined variables as well as to variables defined in the following function block declaration sections: VAR_EXTERNAL, VAR_input, VAR_outPut and var. See Figure 23 c).
    \end{enumerate}
\end{itemize}

\end{enumerate}

#### Deletion of a Location

Sometimes, you may want to delete a location entirely. You will only trigger an operation if the renamed location is the target of a reduced privilege assignment: you are allowed to drop down to layers below the location and reinstall the hierarchy.

The sampr example shows that delegation is not sufficient to prevent an LD APT from dropping down to another link. The link can be deleted if the compromised user is members of another group than the group that has retired.

In some cases, dropping to lower layers is prohibitively expensive or even impossible (e.g., when the configuration is built on a system with low memory). If this happens, you can grant a privilege assignment that reverses the effect of the removed location.

### 6.6.7.2.7.3 OVERRIEDA method

### Page 172

value.A function block type with the keyword `FINALcannot be a base function block`.

**6.6.7.3 Dynamic name binding (OVERRIDE)**

Name binding is the association of a method name or function block name with a method or a function block type body implementation and is used as defined in 6.6.5.6 also for methods of function block types.

**6.6.7.4 Method call of own and base FB (THIS, SUPER) and polymorphism**

To access a method defined inside or outside the own function block type there are the keywords `THISAND SUPERavailable`.

**6.6.7.5 ABSTRACTfunction block type and ABSTRACTmethod**

The `ABSTRACTmodifier can also be used with function blocks. The implementer shall declare the implementation of these features.

**6.6.7.6 Method access specifiers (PROTECTED, PUBLIC, PRIVATE, INTERNAL)**

For each method it shall be defined from where the call of the method is permitted, as defined for classes.

**6.6.7.7 Variable access specifiers (PROTECTED, PUBLIC, PRIVATE, INTERNAL)**

For the `VARsection it shall be defined from where the access of the variables of this section is permitted, as defined for classes.

The access to input and output variables is implicitly always `PUBLIC, therefore no access specifier is used on input and output variable sections. Output variables are implicitly read-only. In-out variables can only be used in the function block type body and within the call statement. The access to variables of the `VAR_EXTERNAL section is implicitly always `PROTECTED; therefore, no access specifier shall be used on these variables.

**6.6.8 Polymorphism**

**6.6.8.1 General**

The cases of 6.6.8.2 to 6.6.8.5 are subject to polymorphism.

**6.6.8.2 Polymorphism with INTERFACE**

Since an interface cannot be instantiated, only derived types can be assigned to an interface reference. Thus, any call of a method via an interface reference is a case of dynamic binding.

**6.6.8.3 Polymorphism with VAR_IN_OUT**

An in-out variable of a function block type, class type or interface type can be assigned an instance of a derived type if the derived type has no additional in-out variables. Whether or not an instance of a derived function block type with additional input and output variables can be assigned is implementer specific.

Thus, the call of a function block and the call of methods via a `VAR_IN_OUT-instance are cases of dynamic binding.

ҳ.If any part of a program organization unit is partitioned into SFC elements, the entire program organization unit shall be so partitioned. If no SFC partitioning is given for a program organization unit, the entire program organization unit shall be considered to be a single action which executes under the control of the calling entity.

**6.7.2 Steps**

A step represents a situation in which the behaviour of a program organization unit with respect to its inputs and outputs follows a set of rules defined by the associated actions of the step. A step is either active or inactive. At any given moment, the state of the program organization unit is defined by the set of active steps and the values of its internal variables.

As shown in Table 55, a step shall be represented graphically by a block containing a step name in the form of an identifier or textually by a STEP...END_STE P construction. The directed link into the step can be represented graphically by a vertical line attached to the top of the step. The directed link(s) out of the step can be represented by a vertical line attached to the bottom of the step. Alternatively, the directed links can be represented textually by the TRANSITION... END_TRANSITION construct.

The step flag (active or inactive state of a step) can be represented by the logic value of a Boolean structure element ’>’, ‘<’, where ’>’ is the step name, as shown in Table 55. This Boolean variable has the value 1 when the corresponding step is active and 0 when it is inactive. The state of this variable is available for graphical connection at the right side of the step as shown in Table 55.

Similarly, the elapsed time, ’*,*,’ T, since initiation of a step can be represented by a structure element of type TIME, as shown in Table 55. When a step is deactivated, the value of the step elapsed time shall remain at the value it had when the step was deactivated. When a step is activated, the value of the step elapsed time shall be reset to 1@0s.

The scope of step names, step flags, and step times shall be local to the program organization unit in which the steps appear.

The initial state of the program organization unit is represented by the initial values of its internal and output variables, and by its set of initial steps, i.e., the steps which are initially active. Each SFC network, or its textual equivalent, shall have exactly one initial step.

An initial step can be drawn graphically with double lines for the borders. When the character set defined in 6.1.1 is used for drawing, the initial step shall be drawn as shown in Table 55.

For system initialization the default initial elapsed time for steps is t@0s, and the default initial state is Boot@0for ordinary steps and Boot@1for initial steps. However, when an instance of a function block or a program is declared to be retentive for instance the states and (if supported) elapsed times of all steps contained in the program or function block shall be treated as retentive for system initialization.

The maximum number of steps per SFC and the precision of step elapsed time are implementer specific.

It shall be an error if:

1) an SFC network does not contain exactly one initial step;
2) a user program attempts to assign a value directly to the step state or the step time.

For instance, side-effect-free functions do not assign values to global variables, to in-out variables, to output variables, to instance variables or to dereferenced expressions. They also do not call functions that have side effects. The same holds true for methods and function block bodies.

\textbf{NOTE 2} The demand for absence of side effects guarantees that the evaluation order of transition conditions and even their redundant evaluation has no effect on the SFC's behaviour.\*\*

*The maximum number of transitions per SFC and per step is implementer specific.\*\*

# Action control
The control of actions shall be functionally equivalent to the application of the following rules:

# Associated with each action shall be the functional equivalent of an instance of the ACTION_CONTROL function block defined in Figure 25 and Figure 26. If the action is declared as a Boolean variable, the OUTPUT of this block shall be the state of this Boolean variable. If the action is declared as a collection of statements or networks, then this collection shall be executed continually while the A (activation) output of the ACTION_CONTROL function block stands at BOOL#1. In this case, the state of the output Q (called the action flag) can be accessed within the action by reading a read-only Boolean variable which has the form of a reference to the OUTPUT of a function block instance whose instance name is the same as the corresponding action name, for example, ACTION1.Q.

# The implementer may opt for a simpler implementation as shown in Figure 26 b). In this case, if the action is declared as a collection of statements or networks, then this collection shall be executed continually while the Q output of the ACTION_CONTROL function block stands at BOOL#1. In any case, the implementer shall specify which one of the features given in Table 61 is supported.

# NOTE 1 The condition Q=FALSE will ordinarily be used by an action to determine that it is being executed for the final time during its current activation.

# NOTE 2 The value of AWILL be TRUE for only one execution of an action called by a PI or PO qualifier. For all other qualifiers, AWILL be true for one additional execution following the failing edge of Q.

# NOTE 3 Access to the functional equivalent of the Qor Aoutputs of an ACTION_CONTROL function block from outside of the associated action is an implementer specific feature.

# a) A Boolean input to the ACTION_CONTROL function block for an action shall be said to have an association with a step or with an action block, if the corresponding qualifier is equivalent to the input name (N, R, S, L, D, P, PO, P1, SD, DS, or SL). The association shall be said to be active if the associated step is active, or if the associated action block's input has the value BOOL#1. The active associations of an action are equivalent to the set of active associations of all inputs to its ACTION_CONTROL function block.

# A Boolean input to an ACTION_CONTROL function block shall have the value BOOL#1 if it has at least one active association and the value BOOL#0 otherwise.

# c) The value of the Tinput to an ACTION_CONTROL function block shall be the value of the duration portion of a time-related qualifier (L, D, SD, DS, or SL) of an active association. If no such association exists, the value of the Tinput shall be ±0s.

# d) It shall be an error if one or more of the following conditions exist:

- More than one active association of an action has a time-related qualifier (L, D, SD, DS, or SL).
- The SDinput to an ACTION_CONTROL function block has the BOOL#1 when the Qoutput of its SL_FFblock has the value BOOL#1.
- The SLinput to an ACTION_CONTROL function block has the value BOOL#1 when the Q1 output of its SD_FFblock has the value BOOL#1.

# e) It is not required that the ACTION_CONTROL function block itself be implemented, but only that the control of actions be equivalent to the preceding rules. Only those portions of the action control appropriate to a particular action need be instantiated, as illustrated in Figure 27. In particular, note that simple MOVE=":=" and Boolean ORfunctions suffice for control of Boolean variable actions if the latter's associations have only "N" qualifiers.

**Figure 25 and Figure 26 summarize the parameter interface and the body of the ACTION_CONTROL function block. Figure 27 shows an example of the action control.**

-responsive system for structured query induction.6.8.2 TasksFor the purposes of this document, a task is defined as an execution control element which is capable of calling, either on a periodic basis or upon the occurrence of the rising edge of a specified Boolean variable, the execution of a set of program organization units, which can include programs and function blocks whose instances are specified in the declaration of programs.

The maximum number of tasks per resource and task interval resolution is implementer specific.

Tasks and their association with program organization units can be represented graphically or textually using the WITN construction, as shown in Table 64, as part of resources within configurations. The task shall execute the associated instances in the same order as their textual declaration according to Table 63. In case of graphical declaration according to Table 64 the implementation shall provide specific means to define the execution order.

A task is implicitly enabled or disabled by its associated resource according to the mechanisms. The control of program organization units by enabled tasks shall conform to the following rules:

a) The associated program organization units shall be scheduled for execution upon each rising edge of the SINGLEinput of the task.

b) If the INTERVAL input is non-zero, the associated program organization units shall be scheduled for execution periodically at the specified interval as long as the SINGLEinput stands at zero (0). If the INTERVALinput is zero (the default value), no periodic scheduling of the associated program organization units shall occur.

c) The PRIORITYinput of a task establishes the scheduling priority of the associated program organization units, with zero (0) being highest priority and successively lower priorities having successively higher numeric values. As shown in Table 64, the priority of a program organization unit (that is, the priority of its associated task) can be used for pre-emptive or non-pre-emptive scheduling.

- In non-pre-emptive scheduling, processing power becomes available on a resource when execution of a program organization unit or operating system function is complete. When processing power is available, the program organization unit with highest scheduled priority shall begin execution. If more than one program organization unit is waiting at the highest scheduled priority, then the program organization unit with the longest waiting time at the highest scheduled priority shall be executed.

- In pre-emptive scheduling, when a program organization unit is scheduled, it can interrupt the execution of a program organization unit of lower priority on the same resource, that is, the execution of the lower-priority unit can be suspended until the execution of the higher-priority unit is completed. A program organization unit shall not interrupt the execution of another unit of the same or higher priority.

Depending on schedule priorities, a program organization unit might not begin execution at the instant it is scheduled. However, in the examples shown in Table 64, all program organization units meet their deadlines, that is, they all complete execution before being scheduled for re-execution. The implementer shall provide information to enable the user to determine whether all deadlines will be met in a proposed configuration.

d) A program with no task association shall have the lowest system priority. Any such program shall be scheduled for execution upon starting of its resource and shall be re-scheduled for execution as soon as its execution terminates.

e) When a function block instance is associated with a task, its execution shall be under the exclusive control of the task, independent of the rules of evaluation of the program organization unit in which the task-associated function block instance is declared.

placeholder où l'édition mobilisait les details.

Exécution de la fonction block instance is not directly associated with a task shall follow the normal rules for the order of evaluation of language elements for the program organization unit (which can itself be under the control of a task) in which the function block instance is declared.

NOTE 1 Class instances cannot be associated with a task.

NOTE 2 The methods of a function block or of a class are executed in the POU they are called.

The execution of function blocks within a program shall be synchronized to ensure that data concurrency is achieved according to the following rules:
- If a function block receives more than one input from another function block, then when the former is executed, all inputs from the latter shall represent the results of the same evaluation.
- If two or more function blocks receive inputs from the same function block, and if the destination function blocks are all explicitly or implicitly associated with the same task, then the inputs to all such destination function blocks at the time of their evaluation shall represent the results of the same evaluation of the source function block.

Provision shall be made for storage of the outputs of functions or function blocks which have explicit task associations, or which are used as inputs to program organization units which have explicit task associations, as necessary to satisfy the rules given above.

It shall be an error if a task fails to be scheduled or to meet its execution deadline because of excessive resource requirements or other task scheduling conflicts.

6.9.3 **Object-oriented mutex**

In an implementer's approach, an object-oriented mutex is used to synchronize access to the critical section of the data type or function. The following code demonstrates an excerpt of such a design:
```python from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import threading

class Mutex:
    """
    Class representing a mutex class, designed to offer simplified mutex implementation using a single thread.
    """
    def __init__(self, value=0):
        self._value = value
        self._mutex_status = threading.Lock()

    def acquire(self):
        """
        Acquires the mutex.
        """
        with self._mutex_status:
            self._mutex_status.acquire()
            self._value += 1
            if self._mutex_status.isLocked():
                raise RuntimeError("Another thread acquired the mutex before releasing it.")
            # Sample code to wait for a specific duration using sleep
            time.sleep(0.1)

    def release(self):
        """
        Releases the mutex.
        """
        with self._mutex_status:
            print("Releasing the mutex...")
            self._mutex_status.acquire()
            self._value -= 1
            self._mutex_status.release()
```

7.2.3.4.3 WHILE

The WHILEstatement causes execution of the sequence of statements up to the END_WHILE keyword.

The statements are repeatedly executed until the associated Boolean expression is false. If the
expression is initially false, then the group of statements is not executed at all.

For instance, the FOR...END_FOR example can be rewritten using the WHILE...END_WHILE
construction shown in Table 71.

7.2.3.4.4 REPEAT

The REPEAT statement causes the sequence of statements up to the UNTIL keyword to be executed
repeatedly (and at least once) until the associated Boolean condition is true.

For instance, the WHILE...END_WHILE example can be rewritten using the
WHILE ...END_WHILEconstruct also shown in Table 71.

7.2.3.4.5 CONTINUE

The CONTINUEstatement shall be used to jump over the remaining statements of the iteration loop in
which the CONTINUEls located after the last statement of the loop right before the loop terminator
(END_FOR, END_WHILE, or END_REPEAT).

7.2.3.4.6 EXIT

The EXITstatement shall be used to terminate iterations before the termination condition is satisfied.

8.1.4 Direction of flow in networks

A network is defined as a maximal set of interconnected graphical elements, excluding the left and right rails in the case of networks in the LD language. Provision shall be made to associate with each network or group of networks in a graphical language a network label delimited on the right by a colon “:”. This label shall have the form of an identifier or an unsigned decimal integer. The scope of a network and its label shall be local to the program organization unit in which the network is located.

Graphical languages are used to represent the flow of a conceptual quantity through one or more networks representing a control plan, that is:
- Power flow,
  analogous to the flow of electric power in an electromechanical relay system, typically used in relay ladder diagrams.
  Power flow in the LD language shall be from left to right.
- Signal flow,
  analogous to the flow of signals between elements of a signal processing system, typically used in function block diagrams.
  Signal flow in the FBD language shall be from the output (right-hand) side of a function or function block to the input (left-hand) side of the function or function block(s) so connected.
- Activity flow,
  analogous to the flow of control between elements of an organization, or between the steps of an electromechanical sequencer, typically used in sequential function charts.
  Activity flow between the SFC elements shall be from the bottom of a step through the appropriate transition to the top of the corresponding successor step(s).

#### 8.2.2 Power rails  

As shown in Table 73, the LD network shall be delimited on the left by a vertical line known as the left power rail, and on the right by a vertical line known as the right power rail. The right power rail may be explicit or implied.  

<|ref|>title<|/ref|><|det|>[[117, 227, 391, 242]]<|/det|>
#### 8.2.3 Link elements and states  

As shown in Table 73, link elements can be horizontal or vertical. The state of the link element shall be denoted on or OFF, corresponding to the literal Boolean values TRUE (1) or FALSE (0), respectively. The term link state shall be synonymous with the term power flow.  

The state of the left rail shall be considered ONat all times. No state is defined for the right rail.  

A horizontal link element shall be indicated by a horizontal line. A horizontal link element transmits the state of the element on its immediate left to the element on its immediate right.  

The vertical link element shall consist of a vertical line intersecting with one or more horizontal link elements on each side. The state of the vertical link shall represent the inclusive OR of the ONstates of the horizontal links on its left side, that is, the state of the vertical link shall be:  

● OFFif the states of all the attached horizontal links to its left are OFF; ● ONif the state of one or more of the attached horizontal links to its left is ON.  

The state of the vertical link shall be copied to all of the attached horizontal links on its right. The state of the vertical link shall not be copied to any of the attached horizontal links on its left.

#### 8.2.4 Contacts  

A contact is an element which imparts a state to the horizontal link on its right side which is equal to the Boolean AND of the state of the horizontal link at its left side with an appropriate function of an associated Boolean input, output, or memory variable. A contact does not modify the value of the associated Boolean variable. Standard contact symbols are given in Table 74.

### 8.3 Function block diagram (FBD)

#### 8.3.1 General

Subclause 8.3 defines FBD, a graphical language for the programming of programmable con-trollers which is consistent, as far as possible, with IEC 60617. Where conflicts exist between this document and IEC 60617, the provisions of this document shall apply for the programming of programmable controllers in the FBD language.

#### 8.3.2 Combination of elements

Elements of the FBD language shall be interconnected by signal flow lines following the conventions of 8.1.4.

Outputs of function blocks shall not be connected together. In particular, the wired-orconstruct of the LD language is not allowed in the FBD language; an explicit Boolean ORblock is required instead, as shown in the example below.

**EXAMPLE**: Boolean OR

____ |  a c | __________ | __________ |  +---+---+ | b | | | | +---+---+ | a---| >=1 | ---c | __________ | b---+ | | | | a---+--b---+ | | |a| a   |    a  Weighted OR in LD language | code  

**EXAMPLE**: Function in FBD language

#### 8.3.3 Order of network evaluation

When a program organization unit written in the FBD language contains more than one network, the implementer shall provide implementer specific means by which the user can determine the order of execution of networks that is effective if not affected by execution control elements.
